title: Business communication
overview: Communication is effective only when the intended meaning is understood and produces the required response. You need to select among spoken, written, electronic and visual methods, identify barriers, explain how communication affects efficiency and recommend improvements.
syllabusPoints: Explain situations where effective communication is essential.
Compare spoken, written, electronic and visual communication methods.
Explain how communication affects business efficiency and how it can be improved.
Distinguish one-way/two-way and vertical/horizontal communication channels.
Analyse formal and informal communication networks and the role of feedback.

definitions.definition: Transfer of information and meaning from sender to receiver.
A response indicating whether the message was received/understood.
A factor that delays, distorts or prevents understanding of a message.
Unofficial communication outside formal organisational channels.
The route and medium through which a message travels from sender to receiver.
Communication in which the receiver responds, allowing clarification and confirmation of understanding.
Messages moving up or down between different levels of the organisational hierarchy.
Messages moving between people or departments at a similar organisational level.

sections.title: Spoken communication
content: Spoken communication is fast and rich and allows immediate questions and feedback. It is useful for sensitive, complex or urgent discussion but may leave no permanent record and can be impractical for a large dispersed audience.

Face-to-face conversation also carries tone and body language, helping a manager judge concern or resistance. A meeting becomes inefficient when too many people attend without a decision, agenda or recorded action.
bullets: Use conversation for appraisal, conflict or change where emotion and clarification matter.
Use a briefing for urgent safety instructions, then check understanding and provide a written record where evidence is required.
Telephone or video adds speed across locations but connection quality, time zones and missing non-verbal cues can reduce understanding.

examples.label: Safety briefing
examples.content: A factory supervisor demonstrates a new lockout procedure, asks an operator to repeat it and follows with a one-page checklist. Spoken explanation gives immediate feedback while the written record supports consistent safe practice.

sections.title: Written communication
content: Written communication provides a permanent record and allows precise, detailed messages. It can be slower to create and read and lacks immediate feedback unless another channel is used.

Reports suit evidence and complex recommendations; notices and letters suit stable information; contracts or policies need controlled versions. Poor layout, excessive length or technical language can make a formally correct message ineffective.
bullets: A record supports accountability, consistency and legal evidence but can make people reluctant to discuss sensitive issues openly.
Tailor vocabulary, length and translation to the receiver rather than the sender's expertise.
Request acknowledgement or questions where silence would not prove understanding.

sections.title: Electronic and visual communication
content: Email, messaging, intranets and collaboration systems provide speed and scale but can create overload, distraction and security issues. Visual charts and diagrams can make patterns clearer but may oversimplify detail.
Technology changes transmission, not meaning. An unsuitable channel can spread ambiguity faster, while inaccessible systems exclude employees without reliable devices, bandwidth or digital skills.
bullets: Email suits a searchable record and dispersed audience but long reply chains obscure the current decision.
Instant messaging suits short operational updates but may interrupt concentrated work and expose confidential data.
A graph reveals trend or comparison quickly, but axes and aggregation can mislead and should be supported by labels or explanation.

sections.title: Barriers
content: Jargon, language or cultural differences, status, too many hierarchy levels, noise, overload, poor technology, the wrong channel and lack of feedback can distort meaning. The exam expects the consequence: errors, delay, conflict, weak decisions or lower productivity.

Locate the barrier in the communication process. A sender may encode an unclear instruction, the channel may distort it, or the receiver may lack time, trust or knowledge to decode it. The remedy should remove that specific failure.
bullets: Status can stop upward communication because employees fear criticism; anonymous reporting or psychologically safe meetings can improve the signal.
Filtering across a long chain changes detail; direct cross-functional contact or a shared dashboard can reduce delay.
Information overload hides priority; summaries, ownership, deadlines and channel rules are better than simply sending more messages.

sections.title: Improving communication
content: Choose the channel according to urgency, complexity, confidentiality, audience size and need for a record; simplify language; encourage feedback; train staff; improve systems; shorten unnecessary chains; and clarify responsibility for messages.

One-way communication is fast and consistent for a simple announcement. Two-way communication takes longer but lets the receiver question, clarify and influence the decision. Vertical channels coordinate authority; horizontal channels coordinate work across functions at a similar level.
bullets: Feedback is useful only when managers listen and act or explain why they will not; ignored consultation can reduce trust.
Formal networks create accountability, while informal networks can spread knowledge quickly but also rumours and inaccurate information.
Managers should model openness, match access to employee needs and close the loop by confirming decisions and responsibilities.

sections.title: Communication and efficiency
content: Good communication reduces duplicated work, errors and coordination delay and helps staff understand objectives and change. However, too many meetings and messages waste time, so more communication is not always better.

Effective internal communication can align purchasing, operations and sales forecasts, reducing excess inventory and missed orders. Externally, timely and accurate communication can preserve customer and supplier trust during a delay or crisis.
bullets: Understanding improves task accuracy, reducing rework, waste and customer complaints.
Fast horizontal communication can resolve bottlenecks before they stop production.
Communication has opportunity cost: measure whether a channel improves decisions and action rather than counting messages or meetings.

rows: Slow and feedback may be delayed
Data trend, layout or instruction sequence

analysisChains.title: Poor internal communication
steps: Costs rise and customer service weakens
analysisChains.evaluation: The best channel depends on urgency, complexity, required evidence and whether immediate feedback is needed.

analysisChains.title: Two-way consultation before a process change
steps: Employees question the proposal and share operating knowledge
Managers identify practical problems before implementation
The design improves and employees understand why change is needed
analysisChains.evaluation: Consultation uses time and can delay an urgent decision; it fails if feedback is invited but consistently ignored.

analysisChains.title: Horizontal communication between sales and operations
steps: Sales forecasts and capacity information are shared directly
Production schedules better match likely orders
Customer service and cash flow may improve
analysisChains.evaluation: Shared information must be current and accurate; a fast network spreads poor forecasts as easily as good ones.

examTips: Recommendations need a reason tied to the message and audience.
Use feedback as evidence of two-way communication/understanding.
A method's suitability changes with urgency, confidentiality, audience size and need for record.
Identify whether the barrier sits with the sender, message, channel or receiver before recommending a remedy.
commonMistakes: Assuming electronic communication is always best.

quickRecall.question: What makes communication effective?
quickRecall.answer: The receiver understands the intended meaning and can make the required response.

quickRecall.question: What is the key advantage of two-way communication?
quickRecall.answer: Feedback allows questions, clarification and confirmation of understanding.

quickRecall.question: How do vertical and horizontal communication differ?
quickRecall.answer: Vertical communication moves between hierarchy levels; horizontal communication moves across similar levels or departments.

quickRecall.question: When is written communication valuable?
quickRecall.answer: When precision, detail, consistency or a permanent record matters.

quickRecall.question: Why can electronic communication reduce efficiency?
quickRecall.answer: Overload, interruptions, access problems and security risks can offset speed.

quickRecall.question: How should a business remove a communication barrier?
quickRecall.answer: Diagnose the specific sender, message, channel or receiver failure and target that cause.
